items.title: An expected type does not reach a call's own generic through a method on the call's result: `let a: [i32; 2] = xs.to_array().unwrap();` and `let x: i32 = make().unwrap_or(3);` (`fun make<T>(): Option<T>`) are refused "cannot infer" (B424's door (a)); writing the argument (`xs.to_array<2>()`, `make<i32>()`) compiles
items.body: A172's `to_array` makes the shape common: the natural spelling of a checked conversion is `list.to_array().unwrap()` / `.ok_or(..)!` under an annotated binding, and today the `N` has to be written at the call. The binding's type unifies with the METHOD's result (`unwrap`'s `T`), and the receiver call's own generic is closed (refused) before that unification can reach it: B424 refuses a free own generic the call's arguments do not bind, and the receiver position is not a channel. Same on v0.50.0 for a plain type parameter, so this is the general rule, not A172's. B627 is the static-path cousin (there the chain reaches the call and the JS emitter hits an internal error). Rec: a design note first — whether a call that is a method RECEIVER may stay open until the method's return unifies (an inference variable, Rust's answer) or the refusal stands and its steer names the written form (B?1). Sizing S (steer) / M (inference).

items.title: B424's "cannot infer" refusal spells a METHOD call's fix as a free call — "as the call's argument (`to_array<4>(…)`)" for `numbers.to_array()`, "as the call's type argument (`get<…>(…)`)" and "ascribe the call (`get(…) as …`)" for `bag.get()` — where the written forms are `numbers.to_array<4>()` and `bag.get<i32>()`
items.body: `check_generic_bound_satisfaction_declarations` renders `{member}<4>(…)` from `callable_name(member_id)`, which has no receiver. For a method the steer should keep the call's own shape: the receiver text (or `…`) and a `.`, `….to_array<4>()`. The length and the type variants share the defect. Sizing S (the message, two pins); the analyzer core's checks (solver's area).
